title: Training logistic regression on 40% flipped labels with no clean validation set and no noise-rate estimate: out-of-fold filtering
insight: A logistic regression can clean its own training labels: dropping every sample that its cross-validated predictions contradict removes mostly mislabeled data and wins back most of the accuracy that label noise costs on digits, with no side information.
abstract_sketch: Practitioners who train simple classifiers on labels they cannot verify usually have no clean validation set and no idea how noisy the labels are, which rules out most noise-handling recipes. We present an out-of-fold filter: fit logistic regression with 5-fold cross-validation on the noisy labels, drop every training sample whose out-of-fold prediction disagrees with its label, and refit on the rest. The key idea is that a sample's own label never votes on its own prediction, so the model's disagreement is a usable noise detector. On digits and breast cancer with up to 40% symmetric noise, the filter wins back most of the lost accuracy on digits, drops mostly truly mislabeled samples, beats an untuned MLP trained on the same noisy labels, and costs little on clean labels. The study is small (two datasets, symmetric noise, 5 seeds), and the filter does not return to clean-label accuracy at 40% noise.
figure1: Three panels sharing one x-axis (label noise 0%, 20%, 40%) and the same two datasets as rows. Panel A, a small flow diagram in flat pastel style: noisy labels, 5-fold out-of-fold prediction, drop disagreements, refit; two grayed-out boxes labeled 'clean validation set' and 'noise-rate estimate' are crossed out. Panel B, grouped bars of test accuracy per noise rate: logistic regression on noisy labels (muted hue), MLP on noisy labels (muted hue), filter (purple #4E2A84), with sd error bars and the 5 seed points, and a dashed gray line at clean-label logistic regression. The gap between logistic regression and the dashed line is the capability gap that the purple bar closes on digits. Panel C, stacked bars of what the filter drops at 20% and 40% noise, split into truly mislabeled (purple) and clean (light lavender), so that the reader sees that most drops are real errors.
contributions: We propose an out-of-fold filter for logistic regression that trains on noisy labels without a clean validation set or a noise-rate estimate.

We show on digits and breast cancer that the filter wins back most of the accuracy that symmetric noise costs on digits, drops mostly mislabeled samples, and beats an untuned MLP trained on the same noisy labels at 20% and 40% noise, while costing little on clean labels.

We report where it falls short: it does not reach clean-label accuracy at 40% noise, it recovers only about a fifth of the loss on breast cancer at 40% noise, and a quarter to a third of the samples it drops are clean.
storyline: Label noise costs a linear model real accuracy, and the usual remedies need something practitioners rarely have: a clean validation set or a known noise rate. The key idea is to let cross-validation do the work: each sample is predicted by a model that never saw its label, so a confident disagreement is evidence that the label is wrong. Dropping those samples and refitting is a one-line change to a standard pipeline, and it removes the need for side information. Most of the dropped samples are truly mislabeled, and the filter catches most of the flipped labels, which is why the refit model recovers most of the lost accuracy on digits and does better than a larger MLP that is fit to the noise. The capability has limits that we state: on breast cancer at 40% noise only about a fifth of the loss comes back, the filter never reaches clean-label accuracy at 40% noise, and it discards some clean samples. What it changes is the default: a linear model on unverified labels can be cleaned by its own cross-validated predictions before any more elaborate method is considered.

sections.title: Out-of-fold filtering needs only the noisy labels
Label noise costs logistic regression 13 to 16 points at 40% noise
The filter wins back most of the lost accuracy on digits and part of it on breast cancer
Most dropped samples are truly mislabeled, and most flipped labels are dropped
A filtered linear model beats an MLP trained on the same noisy labels
On clean labels the filter costs little accuracy and a few times more fit time

risks: A reviewer will first say the capability is overstated: the paper's digits recovery (68 to 78%) does not hold on breast cancer at 40% noise (about a fifth), and the filter stays below clean-label accuracy at 40%. We state both in the results and the contribution list rather than the abstract's headline alone. Second, the MLP is one untuned model, so the win is over that baseline only, and the MLP is ahead on clean digits; we say so and make no claim about tuned or robust-loss networks. Third, there is no comparison with co-teaching or confident learning; we cite them and claim no superiority. Fourth, two small datasets, symmetric noise only, 5 seeds, one K and C; we make no claim about deep networks or large data. Fifth, the filter drops clean samples (a quarter to a third of drops) and takes about 5 times longer to fit than plain logistic regression; both are reported.
